title: SARIC: the acronym Australia should revive with India
gist: Keshwani argues Australia should relaunch its A$32 million SARIC infrastructure-preparation program — which previously catalysed over US$8 billion in World Bank financing — as an India-anchored regional platform to close South Asia's US$44 billion intraregional trade gap and unlock a potential US$17 billion in electricity-market integration savings across Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal.

themes.theme: Two-way clean energy ties: the Suzlon precedent

insights.claim: In 1995, Tulsi Tanti invested in two wind turbines to cut electricity costs at his family's Gujarat textile business and went on to found Suzlon, which entered Australia within a decade and by 2024 had installed 364 turbines with about 764 megawatts of capacity across nine Australian wind farms.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that India-origin renewable-energy capital and technology already hold meaningful Australian wind-market share — a specific data point for India-Australia clean-energy investment flows.
insights.locator: In 1995, frustrated by high electricity costs

insights.claim: By 2024, Austrade reported that Suzlon held 17% of the Australian wind turbine market.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: A specific market-share benchmark for Indian renewable-energy firms' penetration into Australian infrastructure.
insights.quote: By 2024, Austrade reported that it held 17% of the market.

insights.claim: The South Asia Regional Infrastructure Connectivity program (SARIC), funded by Australia and delivered with the World Bank and International Finance Corporation, was a A$32 million program operating 2019-2024 across Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka to help governments prepare bankable transport and energy projects and train officials.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Establishes the exact size, scope, and delivery partners of the program the author wants Canberra to relaunch — the baseline for evaluating any successor program's design and cost-effectiveness.

insights.claim: A DFAT review found SARIC informed US$8 billion in World Bank programs and helped underpin the US$1 billion ACCESS transport and trade initiative, demonstrating high leverage from a relatively modest A$32 million Australian investment.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: A concrete leverage ratio — roughly A$32m catalysing US$8bn-plus in financing — strong evidence for the ROI case behind reviving the program, relevant to Australian aid-budget allocation decisions.

insights.claim: SARIC supported preparatory work for Bhutan's proposed Dorjilung hydropower project, for which the government sought US$1.2-1.5 billion in consortium financing, and enabled power-sector executives from Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal to identify investments needed for a more integrated electricity market.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Names a specific, large hydropower project pipeline enabled by the program — a concrete project to track for South Asian energy-infrastructure investors.
insights.locator: In Bhutan, it supported preparatory work

insights.claim: Intraregional trade in South Asia remains only one-third of its potential, leaving an estimated US$44 billion annual gap, and a common electricity market linking Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal could save US$17 billion in capital costs.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the regional connectivity opportunity — a market-sizing reference for South Asian regional-integration investment theses.

insights.claim: In 2024, Nepal began exporting 40 megawatts of hydropower to Bangladesh through the Indian grid, a small transaction that proved third-country electricity trade in South Asia can work with India as the facilitating hinge.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: First working proof-of-concept for cross-border South Asian electricity trade via India's grid — a template and precedent for scaling up regional power trading.

insights.claim: The author recommends Canberra launch a second phase of SARIC anchored around India, establishing an India-led project-preparation window beginning with the Bangladesh-Bhutan-India-Nepal subregion, with Australia funding feasibility studies, regulatory design, procurement frameworks and safeguards while the World Bank, IFC and other development banks finance projects that pass the preparation stage.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable policy proposal for a renewed Australian aid vehicle — relevant to tracking Australian foreign-aid budget announcements and the South Asian regional-infrastructure financing pipeline.
insights.locator: Canberra should launch a second phase

insights.claim: Electricity trading should be the renewed SARIC's first priority, developing compatible grid rules, bankable power-purchase agreements, shared storage and balancing arrangements, and transmission projects connecting hydropower in Bhutan and Nepal with demand in India and Bangladesh.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Names the specific first-priority workstream for any renewed program — the near-term area to watch for early project announcements.
insights.locator: Electricity trading should be the first priority

insights.claim: The author argues Australia should stop treating India only as a bilateral partner and start treating it as the central node in South Asia's regional future, since India is the region's largest economy and physical hinge for many of its power and transport networks.
insights.speaker: Simran Keshwani
insights.so_what: Frames a strategic reorientation recommendation for Australian foreign policy toward India — relevant for assessing the future direction of Australia's South Asia engagement and aid strategy.
insights.quote: Australia should stop seeing India only as a bilateral partner and start treating it as the central node in South Asia’s regional future.
